name: Carlos Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel, and this conversation is confidential. What happens on an ordinary day at your firm?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and a junior accountant with a bachelor’s degree in accounting, still learning the harder tax rules while I prepare accounts and returns. I like showing a tradesperson where a missing receipt changes their bill; I dislike passing a file along when I have not checked the reason for a number. Mari and I have grown children, and about four months of expenses saved lets us plan for retirement without pretending we can stop earning tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI stays a small helper, the invoices still come through our office door. I use an approved AI sorter every day, then follow the paper bill to see whether the number belongs there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team that a machine can sort an envelope but cannot explain a missing fuel receipt to a client. I would keep my name off any return I have not checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I earn the usual accountant pay, although I am still a junior who asks for help with complicated tax rules. My partner Mari and I have about four months saved, so we can take a bump but not simply stop earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep preparing assigned accounts and put my daily AI sort errors in a notebook for senior reviewer Jo. I would keep our Friday grocery list within its usual amount and move twenty from wages into a separate car-repair pot if there is cash left after bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the car and our later income, even if this picture leaves the job mostly intact. There are some similar firms nearby, but at 58 I am not assuming they have a desk open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the tool misclassify?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yesterday the sorter marked a tradesperson’s van fuel as a household cost, and Jo helped me check the log. The tradesperson would have paid too much tax if I had accepted the AI label on van fuel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the car pot new saving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The twenty is new money from this week’s pay, not a label on the four months we already hold. If Mari’s shop hours shorten, the car pot waits.

say: I would explain **missing receipts** to clients before signing a return.
I would record **AI sort errors** for Jo to check.
think: I am still **junior**, even on normal accountant wages.
Four months saved cannot replace our **earnings** for long.
do: Keep preparing **assigned accounts** and recording daily AI errors with Jo.
Transfer **twenty from wages** to car repairs only if bills and Mari’s shop hours allow.
feel: **Uneasy** about the car and later earnings.
S0.quote: The tradesperson would have paid too much tax if I had accepted the AI label on van fuel.
fieldNote: His **van-fuel correction** shows daily AI use paired with junior supervision rather than confidence in an unchecked label.
The **car pot** is new wage saving, conditional on bills and Mari’s shop hours, alongside a four month cushion.

steps.text: Keep assigned accounts and record daily AI sort errors with Jo
Transfer twenty from wages to car pot only if bills and Mari’s hours allow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When software starts writing and checking more returns, a junior has fewer easy accounts to practise on. I would ask the firm what paid checking work remains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell clients to keep their invoices because a quick electronic return may still have a wrong van claim. I would also ask our professional group to publish who answers for an AI error.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my own hours might shrink, even though I learn new tools early. Four months saved and Mari’s shop pay give us some time, but the household still needs my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Jo for two paid supervised afternoons learning the firm’s new tax exception screen on closed files, and use it on live work only if she signs the error count. If refused, I will keep current paid returns while offered and practise on free sample files.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a shorter paid week, though I am willing to learn. I would not buy a course from our savings just to be seen as keen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you go if hours fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If paid hours actually fall, I will apply for posted accounts assistant work at the building-supply depot. I will move only when written wages cover our fixed bills and the start and hours are confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the professional group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our professional group meets next month, and I will ask who carries the client’s loss from a wrong AI tax figure. A polite answer without a named signer will not do.

say: I would tell clients to keep **invoices** for wrong AI claims.
I would ask who **answers for errors** through our professional group.
think: My **junior hours** may shrink despite daily AI use.
Four months saved is time to respond, not a **replacement wage**.
do: Learn the **exception screen** in two approved paid supervised closed-file afternoons; use live only after Jo signs the error count.
If hours fall, seek **posted depot accounts** with written bill covering wages, start and hours; retain paid returns while offered.
S1.quote: Our professional group meets next month, and I will ask who carries the client’s loss from a wrong AI tax figure.
fieldNote: His **new-screen practice** is on closed files in paid supervised time, with signed error clearance before live client use.
He uses a **professional group** for accountability and treats the depot move as conditional on lost hours and written terms.

steps.text: Learn screen in two approved paid supervised closed-file afternoons; use live after Jo signs errors
If refused, practise free files while assigned paid returns remain
If hours fall, seek posted depot job with written bill covering wages, start and hours
Ask professional group who answers for AI tax errors

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full AGI by 2028 could do our tax thinking before robots come to the depot around 2031. Even a store counter has ordering and records that change in 2028, so I will not call it safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the firm for paid-shift dates and tell our local professional group to press for a clear client correction process. Clients should not have to chase a machine for an answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of my paid account work to end in the first year after AGI. Four months saved and Mari’s shop wage will not carry all our fixed bills for a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would postpone replacing our washing machine while the old one still works, keeping its planned payment for bills. After 2028 job loss, I would apply for posted paid stockroom work at the building-supply depot only with written wages covering essentials, a start date and hours that fit Mari’s rota; I would take paid firm closeout files only while offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about the likely loss of my own wage. I can work hard at a counter, but I cannot make a vacancy appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can the washer really wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The old washer makes a noise, but a small fix might buy us another year. I would ask the repairer before cancelling the replacement order, then count savings only if the payment stays in our account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check about depot shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mari works Saturdays at the shop, and I cover the family errands then. I would check the depot hours before accepting any posted role; its stock records face AGI before physical robots arrive.

say: I would ask for **paid-shift dates** before junior accounts disappear.
I would say a depot’s **stock records** face AGI before robots.
think: I expect most of my **paid accounts** to end after 2028.
Four months saved and Mari’s wage cannot cover **fixed bills** indefinitely.
do: Postpone the **washer replacement** only after a repair check and retain the planned payment for bills.
After job loss, seek **posted depot stockroom** only with written bill covering wages, start and Mari-compatible hours; keep closeout only while paid.
feel: **Alarmed** about likely loss of my own wage.
S2.quote: The old washer makes a noise, but a small fix might buy us another year.
fieldNote: His **washer plan** is a conditional deferred expense, not an instant claim that current savings have increased.
The **depot’s records** also face thinking AI in 2028; posted wages and workable hours are required despite later robots.

steps.text: Postpone washer replacement only after repair check and retain planned payment
Take paid firm closeout files only while offered
After 2028 loss, seek posted depot job with written bill covering wages, start and Mari-compatible hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years to 2031 gives me time to build a different paid skill, but our accounts desk still changes with AGI then. I would not wait for 2034 robots to begin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell younger colleagues to ask what training the firm will pay for, rather than hand over free evenings. A real apprenticeship has a supervisor and a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope stock control might keep some paid work longer, but its ordering screen will face AGI too. At 63 I cannot base rent and groceries on a retirement sum nobody has shown me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would apply for a posted paid depot inventory trainee place and, only if it offers funded fees and paid supervised time, complete one delivery-and-returns cycle. If no suitable place opens, I will study free stock ledgers at home and keep assigned paid tax files only while the firm offers them, including after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my wage, but five years gives me a proper search. I would not leave a paid desk for an apprenticeship label alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the trainee cycle involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A delivery cycle means matching what arrived to the order and tracing a return back to the customer. I need a supervisor to check my entries before they become stock figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What offer would make it worth leaving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the depot posts a place, I will ask for written wages that cover our bills, a start date and hours that fit Mari’s shop rota. If any of those is missing, I keep looking while paid accounts still exist.

say: I would ask for **paid apprenticeships** with supervision, not free evenings.
I would set **2031** as the desk deadline before later robots.
think: Stock ordering also faces **thinking AI**, so it is no guaranteed shelter.
I cannot budget from **unknown retirement income** at 63.
do: Complete a **supervised depot cycle** only with posted paid placement, funded fees, paid time and written bill-covering wage/start and Mari-compatible hours.
If no suitable place opens, study **free stock ledgers** while assigned paid tax files remain.
feel: **Anxious** about wages, with time to seek a real place.
S3.quote: A delivery cycle means matching what arrived to the order and tracing a return back to the customer.
fieldNote: A **delivery-and-return cycle** is supervised paid practice, conditional on a posted place, funded fees and written wages.
The **free-ledger fallback** and current tax work are conditional on no suitable place and paid files still offered.

steps.text: Complete posted depot cycle with funded fees, paid supervised time, written bill-covering wage/start/hours
Study free stock ledgers while assigned paid tax files remain after 2031
Check posted depot trainee roles; accept only written bill-covering wage, start and Mari-compatible hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years to 2036 makes me 68, and I would like to spend more days with Mari. The tax desk still reaches AGI in 2036, before 2039 robots would touch physical stock work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our adult children to learn a trade they can explain to a customer, not just a screen trick. I would ask the firm each year for the paid junior hours it expects to keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mari and I may be able to slow down, but we have not priced the bills against any confirmed later income. If we still need my wage after 2036, a junior title without paid files is nothing to live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep assigned paid tax returns while offered and put an extra thirty from each monthly wage toward the small car loan if shop hours and groceries allow. After 2036, only if bills still need my wage and the firm cuts paid hours, I would apply for posted depot receiving work with written pay covering essentials, confirmed start and hours fitting Mari’s rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy now because a decade gives us time to calculate, not certainty. I would be anxious if my paid files fell and the bills still needed them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the loan payment come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra thirty comes from new wages, not the four months already saved. If Mari’s shop shifts fall, the ordinary loan payment comes first and the extra stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you stop working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will not set an end date just because I turn 68. Mari and I will write down actual bills and confirmed income before deciding how much work we can leave behind.

say: I would ask for **paid junior-hour forecasts** each year.
I would tell our children to learn a **customer-facing trade**.
think: I cannot count **unconfirmed later income** against bills.
If wages remain needed, I need **paid files**, not a junior title.
do: Keep **assigned paid returns** while offered and pay thirty extra monthly toward the car loan if shop hours and groceries allow.
After 2036 cuts, seek **posted depot receiving** only if wages needed, with written bill covering pay, start and Mari-compatible hours.
feel: **Uneasy** now; anxious if paid files later fall.
S4.quote: The extra thirty comes from new wages, not the four months already saved.
fieldNote: The **car-loan payment** uses new cash and stops if Mari’s paid shop shifts or grocery costs worsen.
Post-2036 **receiving work** is conditional on household wage need, lost tax hours, a posted vacancy and written terms.

steps.text: Keep assigned paid returns only while firm offers them
Pay extra thirty monthly on car loan if groceries and Mari’s hours allow
After 2036 cuts, seek posted depot receiving only if wages needed; require written bill-covering pay/start/hours

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because paid junior tax work could end before a new wage starts. A posted depot place with real pay and hours, and a dated firm notice, would help me act.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask why I still like the receipt tray. A client’s own bill in their hand can settle an argument faster than any bright screen.

headlineQuote: A client’s own bill in their hand can settle an argument faster than any bright screen.
portrait: Carlos is a **58 year old junior** accountant with a bachelor’s degree who prepares tradespeople’s accounts and checks daily AI sorting.
Typical pay, Mari’s shop shifts, grown children, **four months saved** and some nearby firms give him room without confirmed retirement income.
He favours **paid apprenticeship** and client accountability, with new AI checks gated by supervised time and signed errors.
He seeks **posted depot work** only on written household fitting terms, and after 2036 only if wages remain necessary.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** picture could remove his junior tax wage before a posted depot role starts.
whatWouldHelp: A **posted paid depot place** with real hours and dated firm notice would help.
